prompt: Redis runs with snapshots only. A snapshot finished, then two orders were written and acknowledged, then the container was killed with `docker kill`. What does the restarted Redis hold?

choices.text: Everything, because each `OK` meant the order was on disk
choices.why: With snapshots, `OK` means the write is in memory. The lesson's two orders came back missing.

choices.text: What was saved before, and nothing after
choices.why: Right. `rdb_changes_since_last_save` had counted exactly those two before the kill.

choices.text: Nothing, because a killed Redis deletes its snapshot on the way out
choices.why: A killed process does nothing on the way out; the file stays and is loaded.

choices.text: The two orders only, replayed from the log of recent writes
choices.why: There is no log with snapshots only; that is the append-only file of the next section.

prompt: Why is restarting with `docker stop` a poor test of how much a snapshot setup loses?

choices.text: `docker stop` removes the named volume along with the container, so nothing can be compared
choices.why: It removes nothing; `docker start` brought every key back.

choices.text: `docker stop` sends `SIGKILL`, which no program can catch
choices.why: It sends `SIGTERM` and waits; `SIGKILL` is `docker kill`.

choices.text: Redis hears `SIGTERM` and saves a final snapshot first
choices.why: Right, so nothing is ever lost that way. The restarts persistence exists for are the ones that give no warning.

choices.text: The snapshot rules are reset to empty on every stop
choices.why: The rules are configuration; a stop does not touch them.

prompt: With the default rule `300 100`, Redis snapshots after 300 seconds if at least 100 keys changed. 80 keys change in the five minutes after a snapshot and no other rule fires. If the process is killed at that moment, how many of those changes are lost?
An instance of 20 GB that is writing heavily needs far more memory than 20 GB for a few seconds every time a snapshot starts. What explains it?

choices.text: The snapshot is built whole in memory first, as a second copy, and only then written to disk in one go
choices.why: The child writes as it goes, from the frozen copy; no second dataset is built.

choices.text: Pages the parent changes during the write are copied, and a busy instance changes many
choices.why: Right: copy-on-write. `rdb_last_cow_size` reports how much was copied.

choices.text: Redis compresses the snapshot, and compression needs a buffer the size of the data
choices.why: Compression works on small pieces; it does not need a copy of everything.

choices.text: Clients are paused and their writes queue up in memory until the snapshot ends
choices.why: The parent keeps serving clients; that is the point of the fork.

prompt: With `appendonly yes` and `appendfsync everysec`, three keys were written and the container killed at once with `docker kill`. All three came back. Why did the last second not matter?

choices.text: Because `everysec` waits one second before answering each write
choices.why: It answers at once; the flush happens in the background.

choices.text: The bytes were already with the operating system, which outlived Redis
choices.why: Right. A killed process does not take the page cache with it; a machine losing power would.

choices.text: Because Docker saves a container's memory to disk when it is killed, and gives it back on start
choices.why: Docker saves nothing; the data came back from the log on the volume.

choices.text: Because the snapshot rules also ran in the background and covered the last second
choices.why: The log says the data came from the append-only files, not from a snapshot.

prompt: Match each file in `appendonlydir` to what it holds.

pairs.right: which files make up the log, and in what order
the dataset as it was when this log began
every write command since then, in the client protocol

right_distractors: the configuration Redis was started with

prompt: Ten thousand `INCR`s on one key took the incremental file from 136 bytes to 330,188. What did `BGREWRITEAOF` do about it?

choices.text: It compressed the incremental file in place
choices.why: The old pair was deleted, not compressed.

choices.text: It wrote a new base from memory, with the counter's value, and started an empty incremental file
choices.why: Right. The value already includes the increments, so they are not needed; the sequence went to 2.

choices.text: It went through the incremental file, removed every duplicate command, and kept one of each in the same order
choices.why: Nothing of the old incremental file was kept.

choices.text: It turned the log off and fell back to snapshots
choices.why: The log stayed on; only its files changed.

prompt: To start the official image with the append-only file on, add `--___ yes` after the image name.
The machine running Redis loses power. Which setting loses the most acknowledged writes?

choices.text: `appendfsync everysec`
choices.why: About one second of writes.

choices.text: `appendfsync no`, which leaves the flush to the operating system
choices.why: Whatever the operating system had not flushed, up to about 30 seconds on Linux: more than everysec, less than minutes.

choices.text: Snapshots only, with the default rules
choices.why: Right. Everything since the last snapshot, which can be minutes or an hour of writes.

choices.text: `appendfsync always`
choices.why: Nothing acknowledged: each write was flushed before its reply.

prompt: In the lesson's benchmark, `always` cost far more with one client than with 50. Why does it hurt less with many clients?

choices.text: With 50 clients, Redis turns `always` into `everysec` on its own
choices.why: The setting does not change; every write is still flushed before its reply.

choices.text: One flush covers every write that arrived together, so its cost is shared
choices.why: Right. One client pays a whole flush for every single write.

choices.text: With 50 clients most writes are rejected, and rejected writes are not flushed
choices.why: Every request succeeded; the CSV reports a rate of successful `SET`s.

choices.text: Several clients write to several files at once
choices.why: There is one incremental file; all clients' writes go into it.

prompt: A colleague measured `always` on a laptop's SSD and found it cost 10%, and wants to turn it on in production, which runs on a cloud volume. What should happen first?

choices.text: Nothing: a 10% cost on one disk is a 10% cost on any disk
choices.why: The cost is the time a flush takes, which differs by orders of magnitude between disks.

choices.text: Turn on `everysec` as well, so that both protect the data
choices.why: `appendfsync` takes one value; the two are alternatives.

choices.text: Run the same benchmark on the production machine
choices.why: Right, with a client count like production's. The lesson's ratio was one machine's; the decision needs the machine that will serve it.

choices.text: Turn snapshots off to pay for it
choices.why: Snapshots cost a fork now and then, not a flush per write; that does not offset it.

prompt: Order these settings from the one that loses the most acknowledged writes when the machine loses power to the one that loses the least.
trap: `no` leaves it to the operating system, which flushes about every 30 seconds.

prompt: An instance with snapshots only is restarted with `--appendonly yes` added to its command. `DBSIZE` answers 0. What happened?

choices.text: The new flag deleted `dump.rdb` at start
choices.why: The file was still there, 128 bytes, until the next save overwrote it.

choices.text: Redis loaded only the new, empty log and never read the snapshot
choices.why: Right. And the next clean stop saved the empty dataset over the snapshot.

choices.text: The snapshot was from another version and was refused
choices.why: Same image, same version; the log shows no attempt to read it at all.

choices.text: Redis is still loading, and `DBSIZE` counts only what has been loaded so far
choices.why: While loading, Redis answers `LOADING` errors, not a count.

prompt: What is the safe way to turn the append-only file on for an instance that has data and only snapshots?

choices.text: Restart it with `--appendonly yes` and then run `BGREWRITEAOF`
choices.why: By then the restart has loaded an empty log; the rewrite would save the emptiness.

choices.text: `CONFIG SET appendonly yes` on the running server, wait for the rewrite, then make it permanent
choices.why: Right. The base file is written from what is in memory, so the next start loads the data.

choices.text: Copy `dump.rdb` into `appendonlydir` and restart
choices.why: Without a manifest naming it, Redis does not read it.

choices.text: Stop it with `docker stop` first, so the final snapshot is safe
choices.why: The snapshot is safe; the restart that follows is what ignores it.

prompt: Every write to the shop's Redis now fails with `MISCONF`. Where should the operator look first?

choices.text: At the disk the snapshots are written to, which the log line names in full
choices.why: Right. A failed snapshot stops writes until one succeeds; a full disk is the common cause.

choices.text: At the clients, which are sending commands Redis does not understand
choices.why: An unknown command answers `ERR unknown command`; `MISCONF` is about saving.

choices.text: At `maxmemory`, because the instance is full
choices.why: A full instance answers `OOM`, which is lesson 14.

choices.text: At the replicas, which have stopped acknowledging
choices.why: Replicas play no part in `MISCONF`; there are none here.

prompt: A Redis holds only rendered pages that the application can build again. Which persistence fits?

choices.text: `appendfsync always`, so no page is lost
choices.why: A lost page is rebuilt; paying a flush per write buys nothing.

choices.text: None: `--save ""` and the log off
choices.why: Right. It starts empty and at once, and spends no forks or disk on copies.

choices.text: Both snapshots and the log, to be safe
choices.why: Safe for data nobody needs back; the cost is real and the benefit is not.

choices.text: Snapshots every minute
choices.why: Every fork costs memory, for pages that can be built again.

prompt: Which `INFO persistence` fields say that Redis is failing to save? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: `rdb_last_bgsave_status:err`
choices.why: Right: the last snapshot failed.

choices.text: `aof_last_write_status:err`
choices.why: Right: a write to the log failed.

choices.text: `loading:1`
choices.why: That is a restart still reading its file.

choices.text: `rdb_bgsave_in_progress:1`
choices.why: A snapshot running is normal; it says nothing about the outcome.

choices.text: `aof_enabled:0`
choices.why: The log being off is a choice, not a failure.

prompt: With snapshots only, `INFO persistence` reports `rdb_changes_since_last_save:2`. What does that tell the operator?

choices.text: Two writes would be lost if Redis crashed now
choices.why: Right. Those two are in memory and in no file.

choices.text: Two snapshots have failed since the last one that worked
choices.why: Failures show in `rdb_last_bgsave_status`; this field counts writes.

choices.text: Two keys were too large for the snapshot and were skipped
choices.why: A snapshot holds every key; nothing is skipped for size.

choices.text: The next snapshot starts in two seconds, when a save rule fires
choices.why: It is a count of changes, not a countdown.

prompt: Somebody ran `FLUSHALL` by mistake on an instance with the append-only file on. Nothing has been rewritten or restarted since. What brings the data back?

choices.text: Run `BGREWRITEAOF`, so the log is rebuilt from what it held
choices.why: A rewrite is built from memory, which is now empty: it would make the loss permanent.

choices.text: Stop Redis, delete the `FLUSHALL` at the end of the incremental file, and start it again
choices.why: Right. The replay then rebuilds everything up to the command before it.

choices.text: Nothing, because `FLUSHALL` deletes the log files too
choices.why: It is appended to the log like any other write; the files stay.

choices.text: Restart with the log off, so that Redis loads `dump.rdb` instead
choices.why: With save rules on, `FLUSHALL` also saves an empty snapshot, and any older one is older than the log.

prompt: An instance with `appendfsync everysec` takes 5,000 writes a second, steadily. The machine loses power. By the table's figure for `everysec`, about how many acknowledged writes are lost?
The shop keeps its idempotency keys in a Redis with `appendfsync everysec`. Which event can lose a key that was acknowledged?

choices.text: `docker kill` on the container
choices.why: The lesson killed it that way and lost nothing.

choices.text: `docker stop` on the container
choices.why: A clean stop flushes everything first.

choices.text: A `BGREWRITEAOF` started by hand while the shop is busy writing keys
choices.why: The rewrite is built from memory, which holds the key.

choices.text: The machine losing power within a second of the write being acknowledged
choices.why: Right. That second in the page cache is the window `everysec` accepts.

prompt: With both snapshots and the append-only file on, a restarting Redis loads the ___ and ignores `dump.rdb`.
